name: STM32F103T8U6
title: STM32F103x8 / STM32F103xB: medium-density 72 MHz Cortex-M3 microcontrollers with 64 or 128 KB Flash, USB, CAN, 2 ADCs
summary: A medium-density family of 32-bit Arm Cortex-M3 microcontrollers running at up to 72 MHz from a 2.0 V to 3.6 V supply, with 64 or 128 Kbytes of Flash and 20 Kbytes of SRAM. Each part has two 12-bit 1 µs ADCs, a 7-channel DMA, one motor-control timer and three 16-bit general-purpose timers, a backup-powered RTC, full-speed USB device, CAN 2.0B and up to two I2C, three USART and two SPI ports, in packages from 36 to 100 pins. The STM32F103T8U6 is the 64 Kbyte part in the 6 × 6 mm VFQFPN36, with 26 I/Os, rated -40 °C to 85 °C.
key_figures: 64 KB (x8) or 128 KB (xB) / 20 KB; T8U6: 64 KB / 20 KB
VDD 2.0 V to 3.6 V; VDDA 2.4 V min with the ADC; VBAT 1.8 V to 3.6 V
36 mA typ at 72 MHz from Flash, peripherals on; 27 mA with them off (VDD = 3.3 V)
Stop 14 µA typ (regulator low-power, 3.3 V); Standby 2 µA typ; VBAT with RTC 1.4 µA typ at 3.3 V
2 × 12-bit, 1 µs at 14 MHz, up to 16 channels, 0 V to VREF+
HSE 4-16 MHz crystal, HSI 8 MHz RC, LSI 40 kHz RC, LSE 32.768 kHz, PLL to 72 MHz
26/37/51/80 by package, most 5 V tolerant; T8U6: 26
USB 2.0 full speed, CAN 2.0B, up to 2 × I2C, 3 × USART (4.5 Mbit/s), 2 × SPI (18 Mbit/s), SWD and JTAG
VFQFPN36, LQFP48, UFQFPN48, LQFP64, TFBGA64, LQFP100, LFBGA100, UFBGA100

notes: An order code adds the package letter and the temperature digit: 6 is -40 °C to 85 °C, 7 is -40 °C to 105 °C ambient. STM32F103T8U6 is the 64 Kbyte part in the VFQFPN36, -40 °C to 85 °C.
STM32F103x8 means C8, R8, V8 and T8; STM32F103xB means CB, RB, VB and TB.
All parts run to 72 MHz from 2.0 V to 3.6 V.

operation.text: The x8 (64 KB) and xB (128 KB) parts are the medium-density members of the STM32F103 performance line. The low-density (16 KB and 32 KB) and high-density (256 KB to 512 KB) members are pin-to-pin, software and feature compatible with them and are drop-in replacements for them; the high-density parts add peripherals such as SDIO, FSMC, I2S and DAC.

The Cortex-M3 runs at up to 72 MHz with single-cycle multiply and hardware divide. Flash holds 64 or 128 Kbytes of code and data; the 20 Kbytes of SRAM are read and written at the CPU clock with no wait states. A CRC unit computes a checksum of 32-bit words with a fixed polynomial, which can check the Flash contents at run time. Each part carries a 96-bit unique ID.

The NVIC handles up to 43 maskable channels on top of the core's 16 lines, with 16 priority levels, tail-chaining and automatic state saving. The EXTI has 19 edge-detect lines, each set for rising, falling or both edges and maskable on its own; up to 80 GPIOs map onto its 16 external lines, and it catches pulses shorter than one APB2 clock.

The chip starts on the 8 MHz internal RC. A 4 MHz to 16 MHz external crystal or clock can then be chosen and is watched: if it fails, the system falls back to the internal RC and an interrupt can be raised. Prescalers set the AHB and APB2 clocks (72 MHz max) and the APB1 clock (36 MHz max). With the HSI as PLL source the system clock tops out at 64 MHz. USB needs the HSE and PLL both on, with the USB clock at 48 MHz. A 1 µs ADC conversion needs APB2 at 14, 28 or 56 MHz. The MCO pin can output PLLCLK/2, HSI, HSE or SYSCLK.

BOOT0 and BOOT1 (PB2), read at reset, select boot from user Flash, from system memory, or from SRAM. System memory holds the boot loader, which reprograms the Flash over USART1 (application note AN2606).

VDD, 2.0 V to 3.6 V, feeds the I/Os and the internal regulator. VDDA and VSSA, 2.0 V to 3.6 V (2.4 V minimum when the ADC runs), feed the ADC, reset blocks, RC oscillators and PLL, and are connected to VDD and VSS. VBAT, 1.8 V to 3.6 V, keeps the RTC, the 32 kHz oscillator and the backup registers running through a switch when VDD is absent. Every power and ground pin is connected.

Power-on and power-down reset are always on: the chip stays in reset below VPOR/PDR (about 1.9 V) and works from 2 V up, with no external reset circuit. The programmable voltage detector, turned on by software, compares VDD/VDDA with one of eight thresholds from about 2.1 V to 2.9 V and can interrupt when the supply crosses it in either direction.

The regulator has a main mode for Run, a low-power mode for Stop, and a power-down mode for Standby, in which its output goes high impedance and the core logic loses its registers and SRAM. It is on after every reset.

Sleep stops only the CPU; peripherals keep running and any interrupt or event wakes it. Stop halts every clock in the 1.8 V domain and turns off the PLL, HSI and HSE, keeping SRAM and registers; the regulator can stay in normal or low-power mode. Any EXTI line wakes it: the 16 external lines, the PVD, the RTC alarm or USB wakeup. Standby switches the regulator off, losing SRAM and registers except the backup domain; it ends on NRST, an IWDG reset, a rising edge on WKUP or an RTC alarm. The RTC, the IWDG and their clocks keep running in Stop and Standby.

Seven channels move data between memories, from peripherals to memory and from memory to peripherals, with circular buffers and independent source and destination sizes. Each channel has its own hardware requests and a software trigger. SPI, I2C, USART, the timers and the ADC can use it.

The RTC and ten 16-bit backup registers (20 bytes) run from VDD, or from VBAT when VDD is absent. The RTC has a 32-bit counter with an alarm and a periodic interrupt, and a 20-bit prescaler that by default makes a 1 s tick from 32.768 kHz. It is clocked by the 32.768 kHz LSE, the LSI RC (40 kHz typ) or HSE/128, and can be calibrated against a 512 Hz output.

TIM1 is a motor-control timer: a 16-bit counter with four channels, three of them with complementary outputs and programmable dead time, plus an emergency-stop input; in debug mode its counter can freeze and its outputs shut off. TIM2, TIM3 and TIM4 are 16-bit up/down counters with a 16-bit prescaler and four channels each for capture, compare, PWM or one-pulse output; they read quadrature encoders and up to three Hall sensors. All four can be chained or synchronised and each makes its own DMA requests.

The independent watchdog has a 12-bit down-counter and 8-bit prescaler clocked from the 40 kHz LSI, so it keeps running in Stop and Standby; option bytes choose hardware or software start. The window watchdog is a 7-bit down-counter on the main clock with an early-warning interrupt. SysTick is a 24-bit auto-reload down-counter for an OS tick. The watchdog counters can freeze in debug mode.

Up to two I2C ports work as master or slave in standard and fast mode, with 7- or 10-bit addressing as master, dual 7-bit slave addresses, hardware CRC, DMA and SMBus 2.0/PMBus. The pins are not true open drain. fPCLK1 has to be at least 2 MHz for standard mode and 4 MHz for fast mode, and a multiple of 10 MHz for exactly 400 kHz.
One USART runs at up to 4.5 Mbit/s, the others at up to 2.25 Mbit/s. All have hardware CTS/RTS, IrDA SIR, ISO 7816 smartcard and LIN master/slave support, and can use DMA.
Up to two SPIs run at up to 18 Mbit/s as master or slave, full duplex or simplex, with 8- or 16-bit frames, a 3-bit prescaler giving eight master clock rates, hardware CRC for SD/MMC and DMA.

The CAN controller follows 2.0A and 2.0B active at up to 1 Mbit/s, with 11-bit and 29-bit identifiers, three transmit mailboxes, two 3-deep receive FIFOs and 14 filter banks. CAN and USB share a 512-byte SRAM.

The USB device is full speed (12 Mbit/s), USB-IF certified, with software-configured endpoints and suspend/resume. Its 48 MHz clock comes from the PLL running from the HSE crystal. Full compliance needs VDD of 3.0 V to 3.6 V and a 1.5 kΩ pull-up on D+ (PA12); the function still works down to 2.7 V with reduced electrical figures.

Each GPIO is set as push-pull or open-drain output, input (pulled up, pulled down or floating), or peripheral function, and its configuration can be locked. All are high-current capable and toggle at up to 18 MHz on APB2. Most share digital or analog alternate functions; when several peripherals share a pin, only one of them is clocked at a time.

A GPIO sinks or sources 8 mA at standard levels, or 20 mA with relaxed VOL/VOH; PC13 to PC15 manage only 3 mA and are limited to 2 MHz into 30 pF. The current of all outputs plus the chip's own run current stays inside the 150 mA IVDD and IVSS limits.
FT pins accept up to 5.5 V (5.2 V at VDD = 2 V) once their internal pull-up and pull-down are off. They take no positive injected current. Standard pins stay within VDD + 0.3 V.

Two 12-bit ADCs share up to 16 external channels and convert in single or scan mode, with simultaneous or interleaved sampling and single-shunt operation. An analog watchdog interrupts when a channel leaves a window. Timer events can start regular or injected conversions and DMA. The internal temperature sensor is on ADC12_IN16. Calibration after each power-up is recommended. Each enabled ADC draws 0.8 mA for its analog part.

Negative current injected into any analog input disturbs the conversion of other inputs; a Schottky diode from such a pin to ground is recommended. Positive injection within limits does not affect accuracy.
The sensor's output rises linearly with temperature, 4.3 mV/°C typ, 1.43 V typ at 25 °C, and is read on ADC12_IN16 with VDDA between 2 V and 3.6 V; sampling it takes up to 17.1 µs.
The SWJ-DP combines JTAG and serial-wire debug. JTMS and JTCK double as SWDIO and SWCLK, and a sequence on TMS selects the mode. After reset PA13, PA14, PA15, PB3 and PB4 are the debug pins.

PC13, PC14 and PC15 run from the backup power switch, which passes only about 3 mA: as outputs they stay at or below 2 MHz into 30 pF and never source current. After the first backup-domain power-up they are GPIOs; afterwards the backup registers, which a reset does not clear, set their function.

operation.topic: OSC pins as PD0 and PD1
operation.text: On the 36-, 48- and 64-pin packages the HSE pins come up as OSC_IN and OSC_OUT, and software can remap PD0 and PD1 onto them; on the LQFP100 PD0 and PD1 have their own pins. As outputs PD0 and PD1 work only at the 50 MHz speed setting.

The HSE takes a 4 MHz to 16 MHz crystal or ceramic resonator, with the resonator and load capacitors as near the oscillator pins as possible to limit distortion and start-up time. Start-up takes about 2 ms from enable. The 200 kΩ internal feedback resistor is low enough to resist humidity-induced leakage, a point to weigh in very humid environments.

The LSE runs a 32.768 kHz crystal with load capacitors of 5 pF to 15 pF. To stay within 15 pF per capacitor the crystal's load capacitance is 7 pF or less; 12.5 pF crystals are not to be used. Start-up is slow and grows in the cold: 2.5 s typ at 25 °C, 60 s at -40 °C.

NRST has a CMOS Schmitt input with a permanent pull-up of about 40 kΩ, filters out pulses under 100 ns and always accepts pulses over 300 ns. The recommended network is 0.1 µF to ground; any external driver takes the pin below 0.8 V.

Good EMC depends heavily on the application software. The firmware is to handle a corrupted program counter, an unexpected reset and corrupted control registers. Most such failures can be provoked by holding NRST or the oscillator pins low for 1 s, or by applying ESD to the device, and the software hardened against them (application note AN1015).

Voltages are referred to VSS. Minimum and maximum values hold over the worst temperature, supply and frequency, tested on every part at 25 °C and TAmax; values marked as characterization or design are not production-tested, and characterized limits are mean ± 3σ. Typical values are at 25 °C and VDD = 3.3 V; typical ADC accuracy covers 95 % of parts (mean ± 2σ). Typical curves are guidance only.

Example 1: TAmax = 82 °C, IDDmax = 50 mA at 3.5 V, 20 outputs low at 8 mA and 0.4 V plus 8 at 20 mA and 1.3 V: PINT = 175 mW, PI/O = 272 mW, PD = 447 mW, and in the LQFP100 (46 °C/W) TJ = 82 + 20.6 = 102.6 °C, within suffix 6. Example 2: TAmax = 115 °C, 20 mA at 3.5 V, 20 outputs at 8 mA and 0.4 V: PD = 70 + 64 = 134 mW, TJ = 115 + 6.2 = 121.2 °C, which needs suffix 7.
